American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology

Prenatal Maternal Phosphatidylcholine and Children's Behavior and Cognition through 4 Years of Age: Randomized Clinical Trial

Hunter SK, Hoffman MC, Law AJ et al. · 2026 Oct 19
Study Type: Randomised, placebo-controlled clinical trial (single-region, US; 206 women randomised, 142 children assessed).
Key Question: Does maternal phosphatidylcholine supplementation (9000 mg/day from 16 weeks' gestation) improve childhood behaviour and cognition up to 4 years?
Key Findings:
  • Fewer children had multiple or pervasive Withdrawn problems (CBCL) with phosphatidylcholine; the second primary outcome, Attention Problems, did not differ significantly.
  • Secondary outcome: WPPSI-IV Full Scale IQ was higher by 7.78 points (95% CI 1.88–13.7; p=0.010).
  • Exploratory analyses: autism-spectrum-range CBCL scores with language deficits in 1/71 vs 10/71 (RR 10.0, 95% CI 1.31–76.1) for placebo vs supplement. No increase in adverse maternal or neonatal outcomes reported.
Clinical Relevance: Patients may ask about choline supplementation, but this does not support a change in UK practice, which currently has no recommendation for supplementation at this dose.
Limitations: One-third attrition, parent-reported behavioural outcomes and a mostly exploratory autism finding with very wide confidence intervals limit the strength of the conclusions; the authors' recommended dose was derived post hoc and not tested directly.

American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology

Bladder Neck Versus Midurethral Placement of Retropubic Autologous Fascial Slings: A Systematic Review

Konci R, Reuveni-Salzman A, Sirmakesyan S et al. · 2026 Oct 22
Study Type: Systematic review with random-effects logistic regression (61 studies: 13 RCTs, 48 observational; PROSPERO-registered)
Key Question: Does bladder neck versus midurethral placement of retropubic autologous fascial slings differ in cure, improvement, or adverse events in women with stress or mixed urinary incontinence?
Key Findings:
  • No significant difference in objective cure (74.0% vs 81.1%, OR 1.10 [0.37–3.28]) or subjective cure (70.8% vs 58.6%, OR 0.46 [0.19–1.10]) at median 2.4 years; improvement rates were also similar.
  • Midurethral placement was associated with less de novo urgency (8.3% vs 15.0%, OR 0.50 [0.26–0.96]); other adverse events were comparable.
  • Wide confidence intervals indicate imprecise estimates.
Clinical Relevance: For UK surgeons offering autologous fascial slings (e.g. after mesh restrictions), this suggests placement site may be tailored, with midurethral placement possibly preferable to limit de novo urgency.
Limitations: Moderate-to-high risk of bias across included studies, with predominantly observational data, so findings need confirmation in an RCT.

American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology

IVF versus surgery for infertility in women with deep and ovarian endometriosis: a partially randomized patient preference trial

Benaglia L, Vignali M, Reschini M et al. · 2026 Oct 24
Study Type: Multicentre, partially randomised patient preference trial (three Italian tertiary centres), with a randomised cohort and a parallel preference cohort.
Key Question: In infertile women with ultrasound-diagnosed ovarian or deep endometriosis, does upfront IVF or surgery followed by natural conception give a higher live birth rate within 12 months?
Key Findings:
  • Randomised cohort (n=55): live birth 57% (16/28) with IVF vs 26% (7/27) with surgery; RR 2.20 (95% CI 1.08–4.50; p=0.019).
  • Preference cohort (n=75): live birth 64% (32/50) vs 28% (7/25); RR 2.29 (95% CI 1.18–4.43). Combined RR 2.29 (95% CI 1.41–3.70).
  • Per-protocol and survival analyses were consistent with these results.
Clinical Relevance: Supports offering upfront IVF, rather than surgery for fertility purposes, to women with ultrasound-diagnosed endometriosis, relevant to NHS fertility pathways and shared decision-making. Pain and symptom outcomes were not reported in this abstract.
Limitations: Recruitment stopped early at 130 of 206 planned women, so the randomised cohort is small and underpowered, and the preference cohort is susceptible to selection bias.

American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology

Assessing the Safety of Estro-Progestin and Progestin-only drugs: A Signal Detection Study of Meningioma Reports in EudraVigilance

Manuzzi A, Fazio E, Nikitina V et al. · 2026 Oct 24
Study Type: Pharmacovigilance disproportionality analysis (EudraVigilance spontaneous reports, 2016–2025)
Key Question: Is there a reporting signal for meningioma with estro-progestin or progestin-only contraceptives?
Key Findings:
  • Desogestrel-only pills showed a clear signal: 110 reports, ROR 11.11 (95% CI 8.79–14.06), IC025 2.64, EB05 5.79.
  • Drospirenone-only pills showed a weaker exploratory signal: 8 reports, ROR 2.41 (95% CI 1.19–4.89), IC025 0.54, EB05 1.17.
  • No signal for drospirenone-ethinylestradiol, dienogest-ethinylestradiol or levonorgestrel; the authors stress this does not demonstrate safety.
Clinical Relevance: Desogestrel-only pills are widely prescribed in the UK, so this supports vigilance in counselling and in assessing new neurological symptoms during long-term use, alongside existing MHRA progestin-meningioma guidance.
Limitations: Spontaneous reporting provides no exposure denominators, latency data or confounder control, so findings are hypothesis-generating and cannot establish causality or compare risk between products.

BJOG

Cytology and hrHPV Testing in HPV-Vaccinated Women Entering Cervical Screening: A Prospective Observational Study

Cruickshank ME, Pan J, Cuschieri K et al. · 2026 Oct 20
Study Type: Prospective observational study (Scottish screening cohort, 2011–2015).
Key Question: How do cytology and hrHPV testing compare in predicting CIN2+ in young HPV-vaccinated women entering cervical screening?
Key Findings:
  • hrHPV positivity was 86% in borderline/mild cytology and 27% in cytology-negative samples (10,000 co-tested samples). Of 1,352 colposcopy attenders, 184 had CIN2+.
  • hrHPV testing: PPV 14.3% (95% CI 12.5–16.4), NPV 98.9% (94.0–99.9). High-grade cytology: PPV 71.7% (59.2–81.5), NPV 89.2% (87.4–90.8).
  • hrHPV persistence fell with longer inter-test intervals (1,007 women with repeat testing).
Clinical Relevance: Supports cytology triage of hrHPV-positive samples in vaccinated cohorts, informing UK primary HPV screening where hrHPV positivity has low specificity.
Limitations: Predictive values derive from a selective colposcopy referral framework (verification bias), so they are not population-level accuracy estimates; the cohort was also screened from age 20 and received early vaccination, limiting applicability to current cohorts.

BJOG

Low-Dose Aspirin in the Prevention of Recurrent Spontaneous Preterm Birth Stratified by Placental Maternal Vascular Malperfusion: Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Trial

Meliëzer JAL, Landman AJEMC, Gieskes AA et al. · 2026 Oct 23
Study Type: Secondary (post hoc subgroup) analysis of a multicentre RCT (APRIL, Netherlands)
Key Question: Does low-dose aspirin reduce recurrent spontaneous preterm birth (PTB) in women whose previous PTB placenta showed maternal vascular malperfusion (MVM)?
Key Findings:
  • Placental histology was available for 160/387 (41.3%) participants; MVM was present in 44 (27.5%).
  • With MVM, recurrent PTB occurred in 1/24 (4.2%) on aspirin vs 9/20 (45.0%) on placebo (RR 0.09; 95% CI 0.01–0.43).
  • Without MVM, recurrent PTB was 17/58 (29.3%) on aspirin vs 10/58 (17.2%) on placebo (RR 1.70; 95% CI 0.87–3.56; not significant).
Clinical Relevance: Placental histology after spontaneous PTB may help identify a vascular-mediated subgroup likely to benefit from aspirin, but this is hypothesis-generating and not yet a basis for changing UK practice.
Limitations: Very small subgroup numbers (44 with MVM; 10 events), post hoc analysis and histology available for only 41% of participants, so the effect size is likely imprecise and prone to bias.

Obstetrics & Gynecology

Progesterone Receptor Antagonists for Labor Induction: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis

Pellot IR, Darché RL, Pires PW et al. · 2026 Oct 20
Study Type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 RCTs (PROSPERO-registered, PRISMA 2020, random-effects model).
Key Question: Does mifepristone for induction of labour at term reduce caesarean delivery compared with standard induction methods or placebo?
Key Findings:
  • Caesarean rate was lower with mifepristone (33.1% vs 41.9%; OR 0.67, 95% CI 0.54–0.82); the effect persisted in placebo-controlled/high-quality trials (OR 0.58, 95% CI 0.40–0.83).
  • Mifepristone was associated with higher 24-hour Bishop scores, shorter induction-to-delivery intervals, and reduced prostaglandin and oxytocin requirements.
  • No differences in PPH, NICU admission, or Apgar <7 at 5 minutes, but most trials did not report these outcomes.
Clinical Relevance: Mifepristone is not an established induction agent in UK practice (NICE NG207 recommends prostaglandins, mechanical methods, or oxytocin), but these data may prompt consideration of adequately powered UK trials.
Limitations: Safety conclusions are weak because key maternal and neonatal outcomes were sparsely reported, and the abstract gives no detail on dosing heterogeneity or comparator variation across trials.

Ultrasound in Obstetrics & Gynecology

Regional growth patterns of fetal corpus callosum at 18-32 weeks' gestation assessed by three-dimensional transvaginal neurosonography

Chen Y, Liao Y, Zhang Q et al. · 2026 Oct 21
Study Type: Combined prospective (Hong Kong) and retrospective (Osaka) cohort study establishing normative biometry (n=956 fetuses).
Key Question: What are the normal region-specific growth trajectories of the fetal corpus callosum at 18-32 weeks on 3D transvaginal neurosonography, and does volume contrast imaging (VCI) alter measurements?
Key Findings:
  • CC length, total area, and regional thicknesses showed non-linear growth. Genu and body thickness rose sharply from 18-23 weeks; genu then increased gradually, whereas body thickness plateaued before renewed growth at 31-32 weeks.
  • Area expansion was posterior-predominant, greatest in the splenium (median ~0.40 cm² at 32 weeks).
  • VCI and non-VCI measurements were comparable. Reproducibility was good-to-excellent, except moderate interobserver reliability for genu and body thickness.
Clinical Relevance: Provides a regional baseline for CC development that may inform future assessment of callosal anomalies, although the authors state it is not yet suitable for isolated clinical decision-making.
Limitations: Findings are from East Asian single-centre cohorts with no postnatal neurodevelopmental follow-up, so prognostic value and generalisability to UK populations are unestablished.
